ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF
JUSTICE

(TORONTO
REGION)

B E T W E E N:
)

)

ALLAN  EINSTOSS                                         )

L. Baumal

Petitioner (Husband)  )          for the
Petitioner

)

DAWN STARKMAN

)

Respondent
(Wife)

)           Heard:
December 9-10, 2002

REASONS FOR
DECISION

H.S. LaFORME J.:

[
1
]       This is my decision in the trial of the issue of
contempt first ordered by Ferrier J. on November 29
th
, 2001 and then again by Paisley J. on January 24
th
, 2002.  Mr. Einstoss
brought both contempt motions alleging contempt of court orders by his former
wife, Ms. Starkman.

BACKGROUND:

[
2
]       The parties had a relatively short-term marriage
in that they were married on June 27, 1993 and separated in September 1997.
They were ultimately divorced on August 12, 2002.  They have a son (Jake) who
is now 6
1/2
years old.  Regrettably and
sadly this trial centres around activities connected with their young son.

[
3
]       Custody, access and support issues were completed
by Minutes of Settlement and incorporated into a judgment by Chapnik J. dated May 2, 2000 (the "Judgment").  Ms. Starkman is alleged to have violated the
access provisions of that Judgment on a number of occasions.  Her denial of
access resulted in Mr. Einstoss commencing a contempt motion, which was later
followed by another contempt motion for the same conduct but related to another
court order.  Mr. Einstoss' motions are summarized as follows:

1.

November
29
th
, 2001
- Ferrier J. heard the motion dated November 8
th
, 2001 wherein it is alleged that Ms. Starkman violated the orders
of: (i) the Judgment of Chapnik J.; and (ii) an order of Lane J. dated August
30
th
, 2001.  Ferrier J. ordered that the contempt issue by tried on February 18
th
, 2002.  He also ordered that access continue as before.

2.

January
24
th
, 2002
- Paisley J. heard the motion dated January 7
th
, 2002 wherein it is alleged that there were further violations of
the access terms by Ms. Starkman.  Paisley J. ordered that it also was to be
heard at the trial scheduled for February 18
th
.  He also ordered
that the access was to continue as previously ordered.

3.

February
14
th
, 2002
- Ferrier J. conducted a pre-trial conference that
resulted in Minutes of Settlement, which were incorporated into an order by
Ferrier J.

[
4
]       For a variety of reasons the trial of the two
motions did not proceed on February 18
th
, 2002 and has since found
its way before me.  Greer J. conducted a Pre-trial Management Conference on
December 4
th
, 2002, and so the several matters of contempt alleged
on the part of Ms. Starkman and referenced in the November 8
th
, 2001 and January 7
th
, 2002 motions are the specific issues of this trial.

The Issue at
Trial:

[
5
]       There are two types of contempt that courts are
called upon to consider from time to time.  Contempt can be either "in the
face of the court" (
in facie
), or "not in the face of the
court" (
ex facie
).  Whereas contempt in the face of the court is
one that occurs within the court or in the observance of the court, contempt
not in the face of the court generally consists of conduct calculated to
interfere with the proper administration of justice.  This can often take the
form of a wilful breach of a court order.  The within case is concerned with
the issue of breach of court orders and thus is contempt not in the face of the
court.

[
6
]       The narrow issue to be decided is whether or not
Ms. Starkman's conduct was calculated to interfere with the course of justice
in relation to proceedings underway or pending in a court of justice?  That is,
did Ms. Starkman deliberately disobey court orders and thereby commit contempt
of court out of the face of the court?

THE LEGAL TEST:

[
7
]       Rules 60.05 and 60.11 of the
Rules of Civil
Procedure
provide the jurisdiction for this court to decide issues of
contempt out of the face of the court.  That is, where it is alleged that a
person has breached an order of the court.

[
8
]       It has long been settled that contempt proceedings
apply where the orders in question relate to a parent's access to his or her
children.
[1]

In such cases an examination of specific questions will assist in deciding the
issue of contempt.  The questions are:

1.

Is the
relevant order clear and unambiguous?

2.

Was
the fact of the order's existence within the knowledge of the defendant at the
time of the alleged breach?

3.

Did
the defendant intentionally do, or fail to do, anything that was in
contravention of the order?

[
9
]       It is important to note that the offence of
contempt for breach of a court order consists of the intentional doing of an
act that is prohibited by the order.  It is not necessary that the defendant
intended to disobey the order of the court.
[2]

Thus, Ms. Starkman's allegations that she viewed the orders as only requiring
her to ensure Mr. Einstoss' access to Jake will not of itself afford her an
absolute defence.

[
10
]     Finally, while there is some question as to the
precise burden of proof to be applied, I have proceeded on the basis that Ms.
Starkman's contempt must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.  Given the
possible consequences that can flow from a finding of contempt - which can
include a fine or imprisonment - it seems to me to be the correct standard of
proof.

ANALYSIS:

[
11
]     For reasons of reference, on August 30, 2001 - Lane J. endorsed the record of yet another contempt motion brought by Mr. Einstoss
together with a Cross-Motion by Ms. Starkman.  It seems to me that some of the
findings of Lane J. - as noted in his endorsement - are worth setting out at
this time.  In my opinion they assist in putting this contest into some context
and are worth repeating.  Among other things, Lane J. expressed the following:

I
have no doubt that on occasion [Ms. Starkman] has denied access.  … Oddly, [Mr.
Einstoss] has not written, nor has his solicitor, to complain [about her
ceasing access] and demanding a resumption of access.

*****

Since
May 4, 2002 [Ms. Starkman has been under] bail conditions inhibiting contact by
[her] with [Mr. Einstoss] - and one would have thought that a third party
request for access would have been made if [Mr. Einstoss] felt it inappropriate
for him to call [her]. … [T]he silence since May [by Mr. Einstoss] is
astonishing.  If [he] wanted access he ought to have asked for it, given that
[she] could not call him.  … [Ms. Starkman's] passiveness [about his not
exercising access to Jake] speaks volumes about her lack of a real desire to
involve [Mr. Einstoss] in Jake's life - just as [Mr. Einstoss'] passive
acceptance casts light on his attitude as well.

In
my view Jake is still being used as the soccer ball in the match being played
by the parents for their own purposes.

[My emphasis]

[
12
]     It is of course important to note that Lane J. was
dealing with his impressions of the parties and the circumstances by reference
only to affidavit material.  None of that evidence had been subjected to the
testing of cross-examination.  Nonetheless, as a learned and experienced jurist
he was able to make the findings he did.  His findings however must be
considered in light of the proceedings in which he believed he was capable of
making them.

[
13
]     This trial then was thereafter ordered to test the
bona
fides
and credibility of both Mr. Einstoss and Ms. Starkman and to decide -
if possible - which of Jake's parents truly cared about his best interests and
which - if either - was using him for their own purposes.  Given the respective
positions of the parties, the answer to these curious and vaporous questions
will go a long way to deciding the issue of contempt.

The
Hearing:

[
14
]     The issue of Ms. Starkman's contempt requires an
examination of the factual basis, which underpin the allegations.  As was clear
from the decision of Lane J. - and upon which I agree - there is no question
that Ms. Starkman refused access contrary to the specifics of orders of the
court.  The underpinnings of this case are necessary to my deciding whether Ms.
Starkman "knowingly" and "deliberately" breached the
orders.  I turn then to the essence of the respective complaints.

Mr. Einstoss alleges that -

Ms. Starkman prevented him from exercising access, or that she imposed
irrational restrictions on granting access.  He asserts that her motive
included that she regularly wanted to reconcile and that when he rejected this,
she would shout and swear at him.  And, that this would be done in the presence
of Jake.  He says that she harasses and communicates constantly with him to the
extent she has faced criminal charges for it.

He submits that the court made
the respective orders with full knowledge of the circumstances regarding Ms.
Starkman's non-communication restrictions.  Accordingly - and given his
distrust in her
bona fides
- he wanted Ms. Starkman to comply fully with
the court orders - failing which he could not exercise his access

Ms. Starkman alleges that -
she
did not deny Mr. Einstoss access but rather, she encouraged it.  She asserts
that he uses access to provoke her and to get her into trouble.  She says that
since the summer of 1998 and continuing to the present 2002 - Mr. Einstoss does
not exercise all of his access.  He only wants access if he can pick-up and
drop-off at her residence.  This is, she says, nothing more than an attempt to
arrange circumstances to make trouble for her.

She was of the view that other
means of exercising access was available, appropriate, and within the spirit of
the orders.  Further, she believed it was necessary to deviate from the orders
given her non-communication restrictions.  She believed that strict compliance
with the precise terms of the orders was not necessary so long as access was
being made available to Mr. Einstoss.

[
15
]     Ms. Starkman does not deny that she did not comply
with the location specified in the orders.  Indeed, she admits to the
intentional non-compliance with such specifics.  However, Ms. Starkman says
that it was at all times her intention to comply with the spirit of the orders.

[
16
]     In sum, the defence submitted by Ms. Starkman
amounts to her contention that the orders were about her providing access of
Jake to Mr. Einstoss - and that the location to facilitate this was
irrelevant.  In other words, how access was initiated and completed was of no
matter so long as Mr. Einstoss exercised access.  She contends further that
arrangements for Mr. Einstoss' access in compliance with the court orders was
always arranged by her - but that because of his insistence on strict
compliance with the location specified in the orders - he in fact revealed his
desire not to see Jake.

[
17
]     For the record and by way of reminder, Jake is a 6
1/2
-year-old only child who is now in therapy
for reasons that include the bitter conflict that continues between his mother
and father.  My heart weeps for this child and one can only guess at what he
believes his own role in this sad affair is.  Each of his parents' claims that
their actions are solely in regards their view of what is in the best interests
of Jake.

[
18
]     Mr. Einstoss and Ms. Starkman do not trust each
other.  They each submit that their actions are correct and necessary in law.
As noted above, he relies strictly on the language of the various court orders
while she relies on the criminal non-communication restrictions upon her.

[
19
]     Because the precise words of the respective orders
lie at the heart of this trial it will be useful to set them out.  The relevant
portion of the various court orders reads:

•

May 2
nd
, 2000
- Chapnik J. - "… [Mr.
Einstoss] shall have access to the child Jake … as follows: (a) each Tuesday and
Thursday evening from 4:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.; (b) every other weekend from
Friday at 6:00 p.m. to Sunday at 7:30 p.m.; (c) an equal share of all major
holidays; and (d) such further and other times as the parties may agree".

•

August 30
th
, 2001
- Lane J. - "… [Mr.
Einstoss'] access shall resume on Friday, August 31, 2002 at 4:30 p.m. to Monday September 3, 2001 at 7:30 p.m.  [He] shall pick up the child at [Ms. Starkman's]
home and return him there.  So long as [Ms. Starkman] is under bail conditions,
she shall avoid contact with [Mr. Einstoss] on these occasions, using the
services of the nanny whenever possible".

•

November 29
th
, 2001
- Ferrier J. - "… the
existing access order remains in place.  Child to be made available at home for
pick-up and drop-off unless Court order is formally varied".

[
20
]     In addition, there are
other dates with related information that have a role to play in deciding the
two motions for contempt.  In connection with that, I find that the undisputed
facts related to the dates are relevant in that they assist me in confirming
and assessing the truthfulness and reliability of the evidence of the parties.
The evidence is as follows:

1.

On
May 4
th
, 2001

Ms. Starkman was charged with criminally harassing Mr.
Einstoss.  Upon release on her own recognizance an included condition was that
she was "not to communicate directly or indirectly with Mr. Einstoss or
attend at any place he is known to be at".  This restriction was in place
when Lane J. made his order on
August 30
th
, 2001
.

2.

On
October 25
th
, 2001
(after the order of Lane J.) Ms. Starkman breached her
terms of recognizance.  She was again released on terms that included the
non-contact with Mr. Einstoss.  Again on
December 3
rd
, 2001

and on
April 6
th
, 2002
she breached the terms of her recognizance, and again was
released on terms that are the same.  Ferrier J. knew these facts including the
restrictions upon her when he made his order of access on
November 29
th
,
2001
.

[
21
]     It is to be noted - and in my view it is an
important fact - that none of the harassment and breaches of recognizance by
Ms. Starkman arose out of incidents surrounding Mr. Einstoss' access of Jake.

[
22
]     Mr. Einstoss testified that on October 18 and 23,
2001 he attended at Ms. Starkman's home - as per the court orders - to exercise
access but there was no answer.  He had no previous notice that access would be
denied or any subsequent explanation as to why it was denied.  At this point,
and given Ms. Starkman's court prohibitions against contacting him - he commenced
written queries about his exercising his court ordered access to her lawyer,
Mr. Altman.  Generally he sent these by way of facsimile.

[
23
]     I find that Mr. Einstoss did fax his correspondence
in this regard to Mr. Altman.  I accept also Mr. Einstoss' evidence that, for
the most part (i.e. October 25 and 30, 2001) Mr. Altman failed to respond to
him.  I find that Mr. Altman at times did not respond at all to Mr. Einstoss
inquiries and complaints and that at other times he did not respond in a timely
fashion.  At the same time I am satisfied completely that Ms. Starkman was
being made aware of Mr. Einstoss' concerns and she was in turn instructing Mr.
Altman accordingly.

[
24
]     Given his frustration with not receiving any
acknowledgment or response from Mr. Altman, Mr. Einstoss says he made no
further attempts to exercise his right of access.  Rather, he commenced his
first contempt motion on November 8
th
, 2001.  As noted above,
Ferrier J. heard the motion on November 29
th
, 2001and among other
things ordered this trial.

[
25
]     In general, Mr. Einstoss testified and reasserted
the evidence that he has to date submitted to the court in his relevant
affidavits, namely, his affidavit sworn November 8
th
, 2001 and the
other sworn January 7
th
, 2002.  I reviewed his affidavit evidence
and observed him during his testimony at trial.  I found Mr. Einstoss to be
forthright and honest.  In my view his answers demonstrated a genuine concern
for the best interests of Jake and a full appreciation of how the events
leading up to this trial have negatively impacted on Jake.  The evidence of Mr.
Einstoss impressed me as being that of a concerned father rather than of
someone who had an alternative agenda.

[
26
]     Ms. Starkman on the other hand was combative,
evasive and inconsistent in both her affidavit evidence and in her
viva voce

testimony given at this trial.  In my view she demonstrated that she does not
always put the best interests of Jake first - although she believes she does.
For example, after Mr. Einstoss' examination-in-chief, she insisted that Jake
would need to be called as a witness to say which parent was being truthful.
On another occasion Ms. Starkman - in contravention of the court order - took
Jake to karate class with full knowledge that Mr. Einstoss would not be picking
Jake up - but she nonetheless told Jake his father would be picking him up from
karate class.  Sadly, in my view these are not examples of a parent who is
considering the best interests of her child.

[
27
]     Given Ms. Starkman's conduct, Mr. Einstoss was -
and is - left with 2 choices: he can either fight to be a meaningful father and
an important part in Jakes' life; or he can abandon him to the sole parenting
and wishes of his mother.  He has chosen to fight, and in my view, he has done
so correctly.  I accept that while it may take to two persons to continue a
fight - I find that on issues of access Ms. Starkman is the fomenter.
Sometimes a party must simply seek relief and assistance from the courts in an
effort to stop the fighting.  Mr. Einstoss has done that.

[
28
]     On August 30, 2001 Lane J. properly criticized Mr.
Einstoss for his "astonishing silence".  And, for his not writing to
pursue his rights of access rather than "passively accept" a denial
of it.  Mr. Einstoss acted on Lane J's. observations and he no longer
"passively accepted" his being routinely denied access.  Although
complicating this fact was the issue of Ms. Starkman's prohibitions against any
contact with Mr. Einstoss arising out of her criminal charges.  And as noted,
that complication was always made known to the court.

[
29
]     The complication was that - on the one hand Ms.
Starkman had criminal court orders that prohibited her from "communicating
with Mr. Einstoss either directly or indirectly" - on the other she had
Family Court orders specifying where Jake was to be picked-up and dropped-off.
That location for access was specified to be at Ms. Starkman's home.  What then
does Ms. Starkman choose to do?

[
30
]     Ms. Starkman's decision was to unilaterally vary
the terms of the Family Court orders from her home to other venues.  For
whatever reasons, she decided to use her lawyer, Mr. Altman to communicate her
unilateral decision to vary the access orders to Mr. Einstoss through him.
Significantly, by doing so she has effectively breached both the Criminal Court
order and the Family court order in one fell swoop.  This is but one of many
illustrations of her complete disregard for any orders of the court - that is,
unless they reflect her own wishes.

[
31
]     I find that Mr. Einstoss was appropriately writing
to Ms. Starkman's lawyer, Mr. Altman, and that this was prudent on his part
given the then criminal prohibition against her contacting him.  Given he had
little to no other alternative, his efforts to express his wishes through Mr.
Altman were both suitable and correct - on his part.  However, this problem was
made even more acute on December 21, 2001when Ms. Starkman served notice that
she would thereafter represent herself in the custody and access issues.  Mr.
Einstoss' efforts to affect his court ordered access were made even more
difficult.

[
32
]     If Ms. Starkman made this decision in order to
deliberately further thwart Mr. Einstoss' ability to either exercise, or
question access of Jake - it is devious.  If it was not deliberate - it was
wholly improper for her to rely on this fact to deny Mr. Einstoss his court
ordered access to Jake.  In the end, I find her decision to represent herself
was deliberate and designed to further frustrate Mr. Einstoss' access with
Jake.  Indeed, it put Mr. Einstoss in the position that he now had no
alternative but to bring the further dilemma he faced to the attention of the
court.

[
33
]     As I have now noted on several occasions, both Lane
J. and Ferrier J. were fully aware of the non-communication restrictions
imposed upon Ms. Starkman through her criminal proceedings.  Nonetheless, they
each insisted in their respective orders that access be initiated and concluded
at her home.  These experienced and learned justices knew that pick-up and drop-off
of Jake - if carried out sincerely - did not require communication between Ms.
Starkman and Mr. Einstoss.  If it became an obstacle, the proper course of
action was to return to court and seek a remedy - not unilaterally vary the
orders.  In effect, that is what Mr. Einstoss has done.

[
34
]     In all the circumstances and at all times Ms.
Starkman had only one option: to obey the court orders.  She knowingly and
willfully chose not to do so.  Ms. Starkman professes that; then and now her
only wish was that Mr. Einstoss spend more time with Jake by exercising all
access.  Yet, she must have known that her actions from late October 2001
through December 2001 were having the opposite effect.  The fact is, directly
as a consequence of her conduct, Jake was not seeing his father at all.  She
knew there was an alternative and that was to abide by the court orders.  She
willfully and knowingly chose to ignore them.

[
35
]     For all of the reasons stated above, I am convinced
and satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Starkman is in contempt of the
orders of Chapnik J., Lane J. and indeed that of Ferrier J.  The orders in
question are clear and unambiguous in their language and intention.  Not only
is the language and intent of the orders known to Ms. Starkman - she has known
them throughout.  In fact, she was personally instrumental in settling the
orders.  In spite of that, Ms. Starkman willfully and repeatedly knowingly
breached the terms of the orders.  Accordingly, the motions of Mr. Einstoss
dated November 8
th
, 2001 and January 7
th
, 2002 are
granted.  I find Ms. Starkman to be in contempt on the occasions set out in
both motions.

[
36
]     I turn then to the issue of sanctions.

SANCTIONS:

[
37
]     My opinion is: the continued breaches of court
orders by Ms. Starkman are deserving of sanctions that will impress upon her
and others that such conduct will be treated seriously.  This is especially the
case where - as here - Ms. Starkman has known the views of court; has
participated in the wording of the orders; and has throughout consciously and
willfully breached those orders.  She has thumbed her nose at the authority of
the court and virtually dared it to do something about it.  Not to seriously
sanction her would be to weaken the public confidence in the courts and give
substance to her wrongly held views of the court's authority.

[
38
]     In my view, whatever sanctions are to be imposed,
they must in the end also be consistent with and consider the best interests of
Jake.  It is clear to me that Ms. Starkman's efforts have as a motive - at
least in large part - the alienation of Jake and his father.  Therefore, that
must be remedied especially given Ms. Starkman's many assertions throughout the
trial that her only purpose has been - and is - that Jake see more of his father.
Therefore, I intend that my sanctions for her contempt assist her in this
regard.

[
39
]     The evidence was especially clear that Jake
relishes the time he spends with his father.  On many occasions in her evidence
Ms. Starkman voiced the importance that Jake's father had in his young life.
Indeed, her concern was always that she wished there was more contact between
them.  I have no doubt that Jake needs his time with his father and conversely
I am convinced that his father wants and needs his time with Jake.  That should
happen and I am hopeful that this order will assist.  I may not be able to put
an end to the fighting between Ms. Starkman and Mr. Einstoss, but I can limit
the opportunities to do so with Jake as the focal point.

[
40
]     Subrule 60.11(5) of the Rules of Civil Procedure
grants the courts a wide discretion in imposing a penalty for contempt.  This
includes an order that the "person in contempt, (f) comply with any other
order that the judge considers necessary".  Therefore, and with the above
as a guide, I order the following:

1.

Mr.
Einstoss' access of Jake shall be varied.  Commencing on the next scheduled
period of access, Mr. Einstoss' access will be for a period of one week and
shall occur on each and every alternate week.  Each access period shall
commence on the Friday and conclude the following Friday.

2.

Pick-up
and drop-off of Jake shall remain as is, namely, it is to be at Jake's school.
Accordingly, Mr. Einstoss is to pick-up Jake at the conclusion of school on
Friday and drop him off at the beginning of school on the following Friday.
During the summers it shall be at camp or such other location as Mr. Einstoss
agrees with.

3.

Access
to Jake over summer holidays is to be shared equally between Ms. Starkman and
Mr. Einstoss.  Specifically, commencing in 2003 Mr. Einstoss is to have Jake
during the first 2 weeks of summer and each alternating 2 week period
thereafter.  This will result in his having access to Jake for the final 9
th

week of summer.  Such summer access will thereafter be on an alternating basis.

4.

The
Holidays will see access to Jake as follows:

(i)

Father's Day will be with Mr. Einstoss and Mother's Day will be with Ms.
Starkman;

(ii)

Jewish holidays will be divided equally, namely each parent will have
Jake for one day of the respective holiday;

(iii)

The Christmas holidays are to be shared equally, namely 1 week with Mr.
Einstoss and 1 week with Ms. Starkman; and

(iv)

March Break will see Jake with Mr. Einstoss in 2003 and it will
alternate thereafter.

For clarity, this Holiday Access
Schedule prevails over ordinary access.

5.

For
greater certainty, paragraphs 4 through 10 of Ferrier J's, order dated February 14
th
, 2002 are to continue, save and except as it may be required to
be varied so as to comply with my order.

[
41
]     Counsel requested that I consider an order that
provides for penalties for any further breach by Ms. Starkman.  Such penalties,
it is submitted, should include such things as a change of custody, a reduction
of child support, and a fine.  In my view it would be wrong for any court to
make such an order.

[
42
]     As tempting as it may be, to accede to counsel's
request would effectively dispense with a person's fundamental rights at law.
That is, one must always presume innocence until proven otherwise; due process
must always be provided; and any sanction must be proportionate to the breach.
None of which can possibly be known in advance - even if one could no doubt in
a given case accurately speculate.  Therefore, the determination of any future
breach must be resolved upon fresh proceedings - although Ms. Starkman should
be very aware that the nature and extent of the proposed future sanctions are
all real possibilities.

[
43
]     Costs of this trial are reserved.  However, in
connection with that: Mr. Einstoss is awarded his costs of this trial and the
related motions that were reserved to the trial judge.  I will fix costs after
receiving written submissions from the parties.  Mr. Einstoss is to deliver to
me - as well as Ms. Starkman - his submissions within 14 days of today's date.
Ms. Starkman will conformably deliver responding materials within 14 days
after.  There will be no reply submissions.

RELEASED:
this             16 day of December 2002.

H.S. LaForme J.
